In the school hall in Kannur, Mrs. Thomas, the class teacher, asked the class to vote on the trip. “The river fair or the science museum?” Almost everyone shouted, “Fair!”
Maria had wanted the museum since the start of term. She looked at the hands rising around her, then at her own hand on the desk. She raised it slowly and said, “Fair.”
Jomon leaned across. “You wanted the museum,” he whispered.
“Everyone’s voting for the fair,” said Maria. “It doesn’t matter.” She stared at the board. Her pencil kept tapping.
The vote ended thirty to two. Jomon’s hand had not gone up for either.

qa.a: The vote ended thirty to two.

qa.q: Why did Maria raise her hand for the fair?
qa.a: Maria wanted to fit in with the class and did not want to stand out alone. Her slow hand, tapping pencil and claim that it didn't matter show she still wanted the museum.

qa.q: What could Maria try next time she disagrees with the whole class?
qa.a: Maria could say quietly to one person or to the teacher what she really prefers before the vote. Having even one other voice makes speaking easier.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when his hand went up for neither choice?
qa.a: Jomon may have felt torn or uncomfortable, and unwilling to pick either side. Whispering to Maria suggests he noticed her real preference.
